Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Situation2: They develop a floor plan for a new office, ensuring workspaces accommodate employees’ needs efficiently.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was sketching the final lines of the new office floor plan. It was almost midnight, and the deadline for the design was tomorrow morning. I was deep in thought, trying to make sure every workspace was functional, every corridor wide enough, every need anticipated. Then, my phone rang again—this time, a call. It was Sam, my oldest friend, his voice shaky. His car had broken down on the highway, miles from anywhere, and he needed me to come get him right away. I could hear the panic in his voice, the cars rushing past in the background. As a friend, I knew I should drop everything and go. But as an architect, I had a responsibility to finish this plan—my team and the client were counting on me. My mind raced, torn between the urgent needs of my friend and the professional demands of my job, feeling the weight of both expectations pressing in from all sides.
